How would you design a pipeline that is: I make every write idempotent: each run overwrites its date partition or uses MERGE (upsert) instead of blind appends. Records are deduplicated on a unique event ID or business key, so duplicates from the source don't double count. Failed steps retry automatically and the job keeps a checkpoint of what it finished, so it can resume. Backfills use the same code path: a rerun for last month is just ten normal runs with different dates.
Explain ETL vs ELT and when you'd pick e: In ETL you transform data before loading it into the target; in ELT the raw data is loaded first and then transformed inside the warehouse. ELT uses the warehouse's compute, with tools like dbt on Snowflake or BigQuery, and is the default for most modern analytics. I'd still pick ETL when sensitive data such as PII must be masked before it lands, for compliance. A big advantage of ELT is keeping the raw data, so models can be rebuilt or reprocessed when logic changes.
How would you capture changes from a pro: I'd use log-based CDC, reading the MySQL binlog with a tool like Debezium, instead of querying the tables. Reading the log adds little load and captures deletes as well as inserts and updates. Each event carries the binlog position, so I keep order per key and resume from the last offset after a failure. Schema changes are picked up from the log and checked through a schema registry. Downstream, the changes are applied with MERGE or upsert into the target tables.
A Spark job joining two large tables is: I open the Spark UI and find the slow stage, then look at task durations and the execution plan. If a few tasks take far longer than the rest, it's skew, so I salt or separately handle the hot keys. If one side is small enough, I broadcast it to avoid the shuffle entirely. I tune spark.sql.shuffle.partitions to the data size, or rely on adaptive query execution. And I filter rows and select only needed columns before the join so less data moves.
Why is Parquet preferred over CSV for an: Parquet is a columnar format, so a query reads only the columns it needs instead of whole rows. Similar values sit together and compress well, so files are much smaller and cheaper to scan. It stores the schema and data types, so there's no guessing whether a column is a date or text. Each row group keeps min/max statistics, which lets engines skip data and use predicate pushdown for filters.
How do you handle late-arriving events i: First I separate event time, when something happened, from processing time, when we received it, and aggregate on event time. A watermark sets how late data can be and still count, for example 10 minutes. Results are computed in event-time windows, and when late data lands within the watermark the window result is updated, using upsert into the sink so earlier numbers get corrected. Events later than the watermark go to a side output or dead letter table, so they are visible and can be reprocessed.
How would you design data quality monito: I'd prioritise by tier: the 30 or so critical tables behind finance and key dashboards get the strictest checks first. Every table gets standard checks for nulls on key columns, unique keys, freshness, row volume and referential integrity. On top, automated anomaly detection learns normal volumes and distributions instead of hand-set thresholds everywhere. Each alert routes to a named owner or on-call rotation with a runbook. For the most important sources, I'd agree data contracts with the producing teams.
What is a DAG in Airflow, and why must i: A DAG is a directed acyclic graph of tasks: it defines which tasks run and their dependencies, so downstream tasks wait for their upstream tasks. It must be acyclic because a cycle would mean two tasks each wait for the other, so they would never start. Airflow then handles the schedule for the DAG and retries for each task when it fails.
Carrier status updates arrive as EDI 214: I'd parse both into one canonical shipment-event model with the same fields: shipment, status, location and event timestamp. Each carrier's status codes go through a mapping table that translates them to our standard statuses, such as picked up, in transit or delivered. Events are deduplicated, since the same update can arrive twice, and ordered by event timestamp so the latest status wins. Unknown codes and records that fail validation go to a quarantine table instead of being dropped, so we can add mappings.
How would you reconcile payments between: I'd match records on a reliable key such as the UTR or transaction ID. For matched pairs I compare the amount and the date, allowing a tolerance for settlement timing across days. Anything unmatched or mismatched goes to an exceptions queue as a break, with its reason and age, for the ops team to investigate. The job is idempotent and rerunnable for any date, and keeps a history of every run and resolution for audit.
Write SQL to find customers who have nev: It's an anti join. SELECT c.customer_id, c.name FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id WHERE o.order_id IS NULL. The left join keeps every customer, and the IS NULL filter keeps only those with no matching order. NOT EXISTS with a correlated subquery on customer_id works too and is often clearer.
How would you get each customer's most r: I'd use a window function: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_ts DESC) AS rn in a CTE, then keep rows where rn = 1. PARTITION BY restarts the numbering for each customer, and ordering by time descending puts the latest order first. In Snowflake or BigQuery I can write it in one step with QUALIFY. If ties matter, I'd use RANK or add a tiebreaker column.
Conversion rate dropped 15% this week. H: First I rule out a data issue: broken tracking, a logging bug or a change in how events are counted. Then I segment by device, channel, region and platform to see whether the drop is everywhere or in one slice. I look at the funnel to find which step dropped, for example payment. Next I check what changed: an app release, a campaign ending, a holiday or a payment outage. Finally I size the impact in orders and revenue so we know how urgent it is.
How would you measure customer retention: First I define what active means, for example opened the app and did a core action. I group users into cohorts by the week or month they signed up. For each cohort I track the share still active by period since start: week 1, week 4, day 30 and so on, and plot the retention curves. Churn is the other side: users who stop being active. Then I compare segments, such as acquisition channel or first action, to see who retains best.
What's the difference between WHERE and: WHERE filters individual rows before any grouping happens, so it can't use aggregates. HAVING filters groups after aggregation, so it works on results like SUM or COUNT per group. For example, WHERE status = 'paid' keeps paid rows, then GROUP BY customer with HAVING SUM(amount) > 10000 keeps only big customers.
Design a dashboard for a city operations: I'd start from the decisions the ops manager makes each day: where to move riders, which hubs need help. The top shows headline KPIs: on-time delivery %, SLA breaches, orders and active riders. Each KPI shows a trend over the day and a comparison against target. Clicking through gives a drill-down by hub, zone and rider. I'd set a refresh rate that matches the decisions, say every 15 minutes, and show clear definitions for each metric.
How would you set up an A/B test for a n: I'd write a hypothesis and pick one primary metric, such as checkout conversion. Users are assigned at random to control or the new flow, split 50/50 by user ID. I'd calculate the sample size with a power calculation for the smallest lift worth detecting, and run for at least two full weeks so every weekday is covered. Guardrail metrics like payment failures and refunds make sure we don't break anything. At the end I report the lift with a confidence interval and check significance, without peeking early.
Define a 'payment success rate' metric a: Payment success rate is successful payments divided by payment attempts, so I'd define the numerator and denominator precisely. The first pitfall is retries: a user who fails twice then succeeds is three attempts, so I'd report both attempt-level and user-level rates and remove duplicates. I'd break down failure reasons such as timeouts and declines, and segment by bank, PSP and payment app. Most important, separate technical failures, which we can fix, from user-caused ones like insufficient balance or wrong PIN.
How do you know if your model is overfit: The sign is a gap: high scores on the training data but much lower on validation data. Learning curves show it clearly, with training and validation curves staying apart as data grows. To fix it I add regularisation (L1 or L2, or dropout for neural networks), use a simpler model, for example limiting tree depth, or get more data. I use cross-validation so the estimate of real performance is reliable.
You're building a fraud model where 0.5%: Accuracy is useless here: predicting no fraud for everything scores 99.5%. I'd use precision and recall, and the precision-recall curve with PR-AUC rather than ROC-AUC, because the positive class is so rare. The decision threshold comes from business cost: the loss from missed fraud versus the cost of blocking good customers. During training I'd handle the imbalance with class weights or careful sampling, and evaluate on data with the real fraud rate.
Data leakage is when a model learns from information that would not be available at prediction time. For example, predicting loan default using a column filled in after the loan was written off. A warning sign is scores that look too good to be true. To prevent it, I build features only from data before the prediction moment, use time-based splits, and keep preprocessing inside a pipeline fitted on training data only.
Bias is error from a model that is too simple: it underfits and misses real patterns in the data. Variance is error from a model that is too sensitive to the training data: it overfits and changes a lot if you train it on a slightly different sample. Reducing one usually increases the other, so it's a trade-off: you pick model complexity that minimises total error on validation data.
How would you forecast daily demand for: I'd start with a naive baseline, like the same day last week, so every model has something to beat. Demand has weekly seasonality and festival effects like Diwali, so those become features. Rather than 5,000 separate models, I'd train one global model such as LightGBM on lag features, rolling averages, prices and promotions. I'd evaluate with rolling backtests over several months, using WAPE as the error metric. Many SKUs have intermittent demand with lots of zeros, so those get special handling, such as Croston's method or forecasting at a higher level.
Random forest vs gradient boosting: how: A random forest uses bagging: it trains many independent trees on random samples in parallel and averages them, which reduces variance. Gradient boosting builds trees sequentially, each one fitting the residual errors of the previous ones. Boosting needs more tuning, especially the learning rate and number of trees, and can overfit if pushed too far. When tuned well, gradient boosting usually wins on tabular data, which is why XGBoost and LightGBM are so common.
How would you deploy and monitor a model: First decide batch or real-time: nightly batch scoring, or an API endpoint for live predictions. Features must be computed the same way in training and serving, ideally from a feature store, to avoid training-serving skew. In production I monitor data drift and prediction drift as well as performance once labels arrive. I'd set a retraining plan, on a schedule or when drift crosses a threshold. New versions go out safely with shadow or canary releases, with a quick rollback if metrics drop.
Design a star schema for an e-commerce o: I'd declare the grain first: one row per order line. The fact table holds measures such as quantity, amount, discount and tax, with keys to each dimension. Dimensions are customer, product, date, seller and channel. Dimensions use surrogate keys rather than source IDs, so history and source changes don't break joins. For attributes that change, like a customer's city, I'd use SCD Type 2 to keep history.
Warehouse, lake or lakehouse: how would: I'd start from the workloads: mostly BI and SQL reporting points to a warehouse; heavy ML or streaming on raw files points to a lake or lakehouse. Then cost, both storage and compute, and team skills: SQL analysts are productive in a warehouse sooner. A lakehouse on open table formats like Iceberg or Delta avoids lock-in and serves both. Whatever I pick needs proper governance and security, with access control on sensitive data.
Explain SCD Type 2 and how you'd impleme: SCD Type 2 keeps history: when a tracked attribute changes, you insert a new row instead of overwriting. Each row has effective-from and effective-to dates and an is_current flag, so you can see what was valid at any time. Rows use a surrogate key, since the business key repeats across versions. I implement it with a MERGE that compares a hash of the tracked attributes: changed rows get their old version closed and a new version inserted.
When would you recommend data mesh, and: I'd recommend data mesh for a large organisation with many domains, where a central data team has become a bottleneck. Each domain takes ownership of its data products and their quality. It only works with a self-serve platform, so domains don't each build their own infrastructure, and federated governance with shared standards for naming, quality and access. For a small or immature data team it's overkill; a central team with good practices is simpler.
Design the data architecture for a TMS t: I'd combine integration patterns: APIs and events for real-time updates from the WMS and carriers, EDI for carriers that still send 204 and 214 messages, and batch for ERP master data. Everything maps to a canonical model for shipments, orders and locations, with master data for customers, carriers and sites. I'd design latency tiers: near real-time tracking and exceptions, and batch for freight cost reporting. A lakehouse with a gold serving layer feeds dashboards and analytics. Data quality checks, lineage and governance run across all of it.
How would you design for auditability in: I'd keep raw data immutable and append-only, so nothing that arrived can be changed or lost. Lineage tracks every report figure back to its source records. Table versioning or time travel lets us show exactly what the data looked like on any past date. Access control, PII masking and encryption protect customer data, with access logged. And daily reconciliation controls match totals against the ledger and bank files, with every break recorded.
Lambda or Kappa for a real-time analytic: Lambda runs a batch layer for accurate history plus a speed layer for fresh results; Kappa uses one stream processing path for both. Lambda's cost is two codebases that must stay in sync and give the same answers. Kappa relies on replaying a retained log, such as Kafka with long retention, to reprocess history. I'd recommend Kappa for most new platforms because one pipeline is easier to run, unless very large historical recomputation makes replay too slow.
